subjects.displayTitle: The soul’s immortality: arguments, images, and the limits of sight
subjects.introduction: When a cage breaks, the bird is not destroyed; it is freed. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses that image for the body and the spirit, but He does not leave it as an image, because He asks that in divine questions we reason, analyse and examine rather than lean on inherited belief. So the arguments follow: whatever is composed of elements must one day decompose, yet the soul is no compound; the body grows lean, sick or maimed while the self that says I remains unchanged; the dreamer travels east and west while the body lies as if dead; and the sovereignty of Christ still shapes lives twenty centuries on, though nothing can flow from what does not exist. Plato made a kindred case in the Phaedo, where the soul is akin to what is unseen and unchanging rather than to what scatters [1]. Bahá’u’lláh adds that dreams can mislead as well as reveal, and that the world of souls cannot be pictured from within a world of bodies. The journey continues into the nature of the soul, the craft of rational argument, and what awaits the spirit after death.
subjects.arc: Begin with the bird and cage and the invitation to reason, distinguish soul from bodily instruments, examine composition and enduring effects, then explore dreams, discernment, faith, and wider philosophical voices.

order.why: Read the argument from enduring effects together with its invitation to fair-minded examination.
shortened: A rational proof for the immortality of the spirit is this, that no effect can be produced by a non-existent thing; that is, it is impossible that any effect should appear from absolute nothingness. For the effect of a thing is secondary to its existence, and that which is secondary is conditioned upon the existence of that which is primary. So from a non-existent sun no rays can shine; from a non-existent sea no waves can surge; from a non-existent cloud no rain can fall; from a non-existent tree no fruit can appear; from a non-existent man nothing can be manifested or produced. Therefore, so long as the effects of existence are visible, they prove that the author of that effect exists.
This is a rational proof that we are providing, that rational minds may weigh it in the balance of reason and fair-mindedness.

order.why: Open with the bird surviving the breaking of its cage.
shortened: To consider that after the death of the body the spirit perishes, is like imagining that a bird in a cage will be destroyed if the cage is broken--though the bird has nothing to fear from the destruction of the cage. Our body is like the cage, and the spirit is like the bird.

order.why: Establish the reported invitation to reason, analysis, and spiritual inquiry.
shortened: In the same proportion that the body of man is developing, the spirit of man must be strengthened; and just as his outer perceptions have been quickened, his inner intellectual powers must be sensitized so that he need not rely wholly upon tradition and human precedent. In divine questions we must not depend entirely upon the heritage of tradition and former human experience; nay, rather, we must exercise reason, analyze and logically examine the facts presented so that confidence will be inspired and faith attained. Then and then only the reality of things will be revealed to us.

order.why: Consider the Tablet to Dr Forel’s distinctions among intellect, soul, and nature.
shortened: Consider how the human intellect develops and weakens, and may at times come to naught, whereas the soul changeth not.

Should any one suppose that man is but a part of the world of nature, and he being endowed with these perfections, these being but manifestations of the world of nature, and thus nature is the originator of these perfections and is not deprived therefrom, to him we make reply and say: the part dependeth upon the whole; the part cannot possess perfections whereof the whole is deprived.
Numerous and conclusive proofs exist that go to show that this infinite world cannot end with this human life.

order.why: Read the reported question about the self that says I and reflects within.
shortened: In speaking, man says, "I saw," "I spoke," "I went." Who is this I? It is obvious that this I is different from this body. It is clear that when man is thinking, it is as though he were consulting with some other person.

Furthermore, man sees in the world of dreams. He travels in the East; he travels in the West; although his body is stationary, his body is here. It is that reality in him which makes the journey while the body sleeps. There is no doubt that a reality exists other than the outward, physical reality.

order.why: Consider the mind’s relation to place and the analogy with the Kingdom.
shortened: Where then can one find in man this mind that resides in him and whose existence is beyond doubt? Were you to examine the human body with the eye, the ear or the other senses, you would fail to find it, even though it clearly exists. The mind therefore has no place, although it is connected with the brain. So it is with the Kingdom. Likewise, love has no place, but it is connected with the heart. And in the same way, the Kingdom has no place, but it is connected with the human reality.
It follows clearly from these explanations that man is immortal and everlasting.

order.why: Read the body as an instrument and mirror in the account of discovery.
shortened: Thus it becomes clear that the human reality's permanence and influence are not conditional on the physical frame. Rather, this physical frame is an instrument upon which the human spirit casts its rays, like the sun shining upon a mirror making it bright, and when the sun's connection to the mirror is cut off, the mirror becomes dark. Likewise, when the spirit's outpouring is cut off from the body, that instrument becomes idle.

order.why: Keep the sun-and-mirror analogy concise and explicit.
shortened: This perfect body can be compared to a mirror and the human spirit to the sun: If the glass is shattered or the mirror destroyed, no harm befalls the outpouring grace of the sun, which continues unabated.

order.why: Consider the source’s distinction between illness and the soul’s inherent condition.
shortened: Know thou that the spirit in its own station remains firm and enduring. The weakness observed in the sick is due to intervening causes, not to any weakness in the spirit itself.

order.why: Read the combined arguments from dreams, thought, and bodily change.
shortened: While asleep, this physical body is as dead: It neither sees, nor hears, nor feels, and it has neither consciousness nor perception---its powers are suspended. Yet the spirit is not only alive and enduring but also exerts a greater influence, soars to loftier heights, and possesses a deeper understanding.

It is therefore evident that the spirit is different from the body, that the bird is different from the cage, and that the power and influence of the spirit is more pronounced without the intermediary of the body. Now, if the instrument becomes idle, its wielder continues to exist. For example, if the pen is abandoned or broken, the writer remains alive and well; if a house is destroyed, its owner lives on. This is one of the rational arguments proving the immortality of the soul.

order.why: Keep the reported argument about bodily changes and enduring spiritual identity.
shortened: An evidence of the immortality of the human spirit is the fact that it is not affected by changes in the body.

If the body should become lean the spirit would not become lean. If the body should become corpulent the spirit would not become corpulent. If the body should be dismembered the spirit would not be affected. In brief, the spirit is independent of the body, and the disintegrations that take place in the body do not affect the soul, for the human reality or spirit is ever the same.

order.why: Read the reported counsel to a man who had lost both legs in its personal setting.
Retain the reported distinction between bodily conditions and spirit.
shortened: We see that cold, heat, suffering, etc, only concern the body, they do not touch the spirit.

order.why: Argues for the spirit’s independence from bodily injury.
Consider the reported lamp and darkened glass as an analogy for impaired manifestation.
Keep the acknowledgment that an accident can efface memory.
shortened: An observant traveller passing along a way will certainly recall his discoveries to mind, unless some accident befall him and efface the memory.

order.why: Read the personal counsels and the distinction between physical balance and intellect.
shortened: That state of matter which is the cause of the equilibrium and perfection of the body is that perfect and balanced nature obtainable through the composition and mixture of the elements. It is physical and not spiritual. But the intellect, which discovereth the realities of things, is a spiritual nature and is not physical. Therefore, the animal is deprived of it, for it is specialized to man. The animal is able to perceive sensible realities, but man is able to perceive intelligible realities. It is evident then that the intellect is a spiritual faculty and not a physical one.

order.why: Consider the argument from capacities and effects, keeping its animal comparisons and ether example historically situated.
shortened: Modern philosophers say: "Nowhere do we see a spirit in man, and, although we have investigated the inmost recesses of the human body, nowhere do we perceive a spiritual power. How then are we to imagine a power which is not sensible?" The divine philosophers reply: "The spirit of the animal is not sensible either and cannot be perceived through our material powers: How do you infer its existence? There is no doubt that it is from its effects that you infer in the animal the existence of a power which is lacking in the plant, and that is the power of the senses--sight, hearing and the other powers. It is from these that you infer that there is an animal spirit. Infer likewise from the aforementioned signs and arguments the existence of a human spirit.

order.why: Read the source’s intelligible-reality distinction with its natural-philosophical terminology.
Consider the argument concerning qualities of a branch and root.
Read the reported part-and-whole formulation.
Keep the related reported conclusion about power beyond nature.
Consider the reported drop-and-ocean question as another formulation of that premise.
Read the simple-essence argument contrasted with bodily composition.
Consider the reported inference from indivisibility to endurance.
Distinguish the spiritual Kingdom from speculation about souls living on planets.
Keep the originated yet everlasting soul and the explicit instruction to seek the analogy’s intent.
shortened: Know that, although human souls have existed upon the earth for a myriad ages and cycles, the human soul is nonetheless originated. And since it is a sign of God, once it has come into being it is everlasting.

For the world of things is a world of imperfection in relation to that of man, and the world of man is a world of perfection in relation to that of things. When imperfect things reach the stage of perfection, they become everlasting. This is meant as an example: Seek to grasp the true intent.

order.why: Read the reported distinction between material forms and simultaneous conceptual forms.
Keep the related report on geometric forms and limits of perception.
Read the reported sequence joining bodily change, conceptual forms, and noncomposition.
shortened: Observe and understand how this human body changes; nevertheless, the spirit of man remains ever in the same condition.

This is proof that the spirit of man is distinct from his body. Defects in the body or its members do not imply defects in the spirit. This leads to the accurate conclusion that if the whole body should be subjected to a radical change, the spirit will survive that change; that even if the body of man is destroyed and becomes nonexistent, the spirit of man remains unaffected. For the spirit of man is everlasting.

If an elementary substance is possessed of immortality, how can the human spirit or reality, which is wholly above combination and composition, be destroyed? Nay, rather, that spirit, which is all in all, is a unit and not a compound. Its destruction, therefore, is not possible.

order.why: Examine the six reported arguments individually and their shared assumptions.
shortened: But if an existent is not composed of physical elements, it is not subject to disintegration and death. Nay, rather it shall eternally live and endure. Since the soul is by no means composed of elements, it is therefore not subject to disintegration. Every composed being shall become decomposed, but since the soul is not composed, it can never perish.

The sixth proof: When you contemplate or consider any matter, you often consult with yourself about it. But who is it that gives opinions to you like a person sitting in front of you holding a conversation? When you are deliberating, with whom are you conversing? It is certain that it is the soul.

order.why: Keep the reported internal consultation, thought, dreams, and composition arguments together.
shortened: When you wish to reflect upon or consider a matter, you consult something within you. You say, shall I do it, or shall I not do it? Is it better to make this journey or abandon it? Whom do you consult? Who is within you deciding this question? Surely there is a distinct power, an intelligent ego. Were it not distinct from your ego, you would not be consulting it. It is greater than the faculty of thought. It is your spirit which teaches you, which advises and decides upon matters.

order.why: Read the extended reported synthesis and its historical philosophical language.
shortened: Life is the expression of composition; and death, the expression of decomposition.

As the spirit of man is not composed of material elements, it is not subject to decomposition and, therefore, has no death. It is self-evident that the human spirit is simple, single and not composed in order that it may come to immortality, and it is a philosophical axiom that the individual or indivisible atom is indestructible.
Likewise, the human spirit, inasmuch as it is not composed of individual elements or atoms -- as it is sanctified above these elements -- is eternal. This is a self-evident proof of its immortality.

order.why: Consider the seven reported lines of reasoning and their movement toward spiritual assurance.
shortened: Know, therefore, that death does not pertain to existence. At most, there is transition from one state to another, for the soul of man is not composed; it is not a formation of elements subject to dissolution. If it was composed, we would have to consider it mortal. But since it is not composed, it is therefore incapable of being annihilated.

In fine, a person who possesses insight, who is spiritual and compassionate, will discover that the soul of man has ever been and will be imperishable, he will perceive all things in its presence and beneath its shadow, and he will behold himself immortal, everlasting, perpetual, and eternally immersed in the lights of God, the Most Glorious, for he is endowed with spiritual perception and receives heavenly impressions; he is not restricted by the rules of logic or the limitations of human understanding.

order.why: Read the reported distinction between mediated and independent perception.
shortened: Furthermore, this immortal human soul is endowed with two means of perception: One is effected through instrumentality; the other, independently.

It often happens that a man in a state of wakefulness has not been able to accomplish the solution of a problem, and when he goes to sleep, he will reach that solution in a dream. How often it has happened that he has dreamed, even as the prophets have dreamed, of the future; and events which have thus been foreshadowed have come to pass literally.

Therefore, we learn that the immortality of the soul, or spirit, is not contingent or dependent upon the so-called immortality of the body, because the body in the quiescent state, in the time of sleep, may be as dead, unconscious, senseless; but the soul, or spirit, is possessed of perceptions, sensations, motion and discovery.

order.why: Keep the reported argument from transformation rather than annihilation in its conceptual framework.
Consider enduring prophetic effects together with the reported call to spiritual development.
shortened: You observe that one appeared two thousand years ago, and His effects still persist; another was three thousand years ago, and His influences are still evident. Though physically absent, they exist in the realm of the Kingdom; hence their effects are manifest and their lights radiant. For that which is non-existent has no effect--it is certain that effects result from existence. What influence can come from non-existence? These manifest effects that remain from perfect beings prove their existence.

order.why: Read the argument from the Prophets’ sacrifices and convictions.
shortened: If thou wouldst reflect upon the deeds of the Prophets, thou wouldst bear witness with absolute certitude that there are worlds besides this world.
Now if such souls had considered divine worlds to be limited to this earthly life, they would never have surrendered themselves to their enemies nor endured unprecedented trials and tribulations.

order.why: Keep the rhetorical question about returning to earthly suffering in its source’s voice.
Read the reported discussion of sensory evidence and spiritual purpose.
shortened: Those who do not believe in immortality have some proofs. For example, one is this. They divide existence into two kinds; imaginary existence and that of the senses. They say that since the immortal kingdom is not of the senses there can be no such kingdom. This is their proof! By this proof they deny!

But Jesus and Baha'u'llah answer the people who do not believe thus: Every rational man can see that the world has come out of non-existence into existence. Life progresses from the mineral kingdom to the vegetable kingdom, from the vegetable to the animal, and from thence to the human kingdom. Were there no spiritual kingdom, life would be useless.

order.why: Keep the reported dialogue on proof, analogy, and unseen realities attributed, including its limits of present knowledge.
shortened: But then, my daughter, you should not fall silent in embarrasment, but you should tell him: "O atheist, there is no America, I have not seen America, I have not even glanced at America, I cannot believe the travellers and books, I want, here from London, in London itself, to see, touch, count, measure, weigh America, other proofs I will not accept as valid!" How will the atheist reply to you? He will say: "Come with me to America; here in London I cannot show you America concretely, visibly, but there, on the spot, you will have to let yourself be convinced and you will be convinced of the land of America" - and you will reply: "Good, O atheist, but what is fair to one is fair to the other - my thinking self is my soul, and the home of my soul is there with the Origin and Source of all souls - with God.

Now we live in belief, in surmise, in feeling, in delicate, fragile proof by analogy (comparison), in the reflection and refulgence of the Eternal, the Immeasurable, the Incorporeal. -O atheist, I cannot reach down for you, for example, the moon from the firmament, to touch and see close to, but approach the water and at least look at its reflection, the image of the heavenly body. Much can now only be 'seen from afar', imagined from afar, but the day of seeing it close - of touching and possessing, will come, and then we shall speak further."

order.why: Enter the Seven Valleys’ dream imagery as a sign inviting reflection beyond ordinary perception.
shortened: One of the created phenomena is the dream. Behold how many secrets have been deposited therein, how many wisdoms treasured up, how many worlds concealed. Observe how thou art asleep in a dwelling, and its doors are shut; on a sudden thou findest thyself in a far-off city, which thou enterest without moving thy feet or wearying thy body. Without taxing thine eyes, thou seest; without troubling thine ears, thou hearest; without a tongue, thou speakest. And perchance when ten years have passed, thou wilt witness in this temporal world the very things thou hast dreamt tonight.
68 God, the Most High, hath placed these signs in men so that veiled minds might not deny the mysteries of the life beyond, nor belittle that which hath been promised them.

order.why: Read the reported two modes of operation through and without bodily instruments.
shortened: The spirit has two modes of operation: one through instruments and means, that is, seeing through the eye, hearing through the ear, speaking through the tongue.

The other operation is without instruments, as in the world of dreams where one sees without eyes, hears without ears, speaks without tongue, and travels without moving the feet. All spiritual powers manifest without bodily means in the world of dreams.

order.why: Consider the two permitted descriptions of the dream world in the Suriy-i-Vafa.
Read stillness, motion, and the source’s account of dreams leading to praise.
shortened: The soul is a sign that is sanctified from entry and exit; it is both still and in motion, seated yet soaring. It beareth witness to a world that hath beginning and end, and likewise to a world that is sanctified from beginning and end. In this night thou observest a matter, and after twenty years, more or less, thou shalt behold that very same thing. Now consider what manner of world this is.

order.why: Keep the Bab’s sun analogy and affirmation of dreams as signs.
Read the extended commentary with its distinctions about dreams, sources of variation, and steadfastness.
shortened: It is a special world among the divine worlds and is indicative of infinite matters. Among other things, it is evidence of a realm wherein no beginning or end, no first or last, can be witnessed. Thus, something is observed in sleep, and after a number of years that very same thing is witnessed.

It likewise beareth witness to the resurrection and revival after death, even as Luqman said to his son: "If thou art able not to sleep, thou art able not to die. And if thou art able not to awaken after sleep, thou art able not to be raised after death." Even as death is a reality, so is sleep a reality, and even as there is awakening after sleep, so is there resurrection after death. Sleep sometimes varies according to the differences in souls, thoughts, food and drink. In the dreams of holy souls there hath been and is no variation, for they are pure wakefulness.

order.why: Consider Joseph’s dream as an example of different forms and meanings across worlds.
shortened: The most truthful of speakers, in His book, mentions Joseph's vision (upon him and the Lord of our age be peace) and his interpretation of the dreams of two other individuals. Now consider. What kind of world is that wherein his father and mother are seen as the sun and the moon, and his brothers appear in the form of stars? And what is this world wherein the reverse is seen: the sun and the moon in the form of his father and mother, and the stars in the form of his brothers? He says (exalted be his sovereignty), "I saw eleven stars, and the sun and the moon; I saw them bowing down before me." The interpretation of this vision became clear once Joseph was established upon the throne of glory, and Jacob and Joseph's eleven brothers prostrated themselves at his feet.
Now, since this question has become established and ascertained, it is evident that the rendering of each due takes place in every world in a manner befitting that world.

order.why: Balance dream imagery with the distinction between fruitful discovery and delusion.
shortened: The mind and thought of man at times discovers certain truths, and this thought and discovery produce definite results and benefits. Such thoughts have a solid foundation. But many things come to mind that are like the waves of the sea of delusion; they bear no fruit and produce no result. In the world of sleep, too, one may have a dream which exactly comes true, while on another occasion one will have a dream which has absolutely no result.

order.why: Read the perceiving soul’s possible discoveries within the source’s account.
shortened: It often occurs that man, while in the world of vision, receives a revelation, which later, comes to pass in the contingent world. The "perceiving soul" of man is the power which discovers. Wheresoever it is directed it discovers the hidden mysteries therein, and brings to light that which was veiled. Therefore it is possible for man to arrive at the station wherein future events are revealed to him.

order.why: Keep spiritual communication and the dream analogy with the existing source omission.
shortened: When this is purified human hearts are attuned and reflect one another, and thus spiritual emotions are generated. This is like the world of dreams when man is detached from things which are tangible and experienceth those of the spirit. What amazing laws operate, and what remarkable discoveries are made! And it may even be that detailed communications are registered...

order.why: Consider the reported horse-and-rider image of instrument and agent.
Read the personal remembrance of a beloved companion seen in a dream.
shortened: I loved him very much, for he was delightful to converse with, and as a companion second to none. One night, not long ago, I saw him in the world of dreams. Although his frame had always been massive, in the dream world he appeared larger and more corpulent than ever. It seemed as if he had returned from a journey. I said to him, "Jinab, you have grown good and stout."

order.why: Hear the prayer that a dream become a means of love and kindness.
Close the linked readings with limits on imagining the soul’s world and the rejection of reincarnation.
shortened: But in this world all those called into being are new souls. It is not that a former soul becometh incarnated in another person, or that another individual becometh the soul of a former individual.

Understanding the world of souls is impossible in this world of bodies. That world is unlike anything you can conceive in your imagination. In these perishable bodies one cannot perceive the immortal worlds, save through that which ye sometimes behold in a dream.

order.why: Read the supplied account based on Plotinus as a philosophical comparison concerning identity and perception.
Preserve the supplied cross-reference to Plotinus as a reference fragment, without inventing a quotation.
Read the supplied simple-essence passage with its omissions visible.
Keep the supplied Mahmud’s Diary formulation about noncomposition.
Read the supplied provisional account of the spirit’s enduring state.
Keep the letter about illness and the soul’s inherent condition.
Read the supplied argument about conceptual forms with its opening omission.
Consider the supplied part-and-whole question.
Keep the two supplied translations of the spirit-and-matter discussion distinct.
Read the supplied account of inspiration in sleep and wakefulness.
Keep the counsel that dreams are influenced by the dreamer and should not receive excessive weight.
Read the supplied Qur’anic account of sleep and death in its own theological voice.
Retain Izutsu’s account of Ibn Arabi as an attributed interpretive passage.
Consider the supplied letter’s acknowledgment of accepting some teachings on faith.
Close with Bede’s supplied sparrow image and its question about what lies beyond the visible span of life.

questions: What does the bird-and-cage image help us understand, and what would require further argument beyond the image?
Which premises about composition, identity, and thought carry the greatest weight in these readings?
How might we distinguish an inference from enduring effects from an inference about the nature of the soul itself?
How does the compilation’s caution about dreams affect the way its dream-based arguments are read?
What affinities and differences emerge when comparing these arguments with the Phaedo’s distinction between changing bodies and unseen realities?
How might reasoned inquiry, spiritual experience, and faith work together while leaving room to examine what remains uncertain?

references.note: Read the dialogue beginning with the question of what is liable to be scattered, through the argument about the soul’s affinity with the unseen and unchanging. Compare the premises about composition and dissolution with this compilation. Keep Plato’s larger setting, including its account of pre-existence and transmigration, distinct from the Baha’i passages.

subjects.displayTitle: Contentment: a tranquil heart and an active life
subjects.introduction: Contentment, as ‘Abdu’l-Bahá describes it, is not the stillness of folded hands. A person strives in worldly affairs, seeks treatment when ill, keeps a profession and lives on no one else, and all the while the heart stays free, neither puffed up by gain nor cast down by loss. The difficulty is admitted openly: radiant acquiescence is called one of the hardest attainments, grief and tears are given their place, and the Báb Himself speaks of His sorrow for the family His nearness might endanger. What steadies the heart is a relationship rather than a technique. Before a destiny that no ransom can turn back, the believer prays to be made content, trusts a wisdom that sees further than present wishes, and slowly learns to taste bitterness as if it were honey. Epictetus, dividing what lies within our power from what does not, offers a philosopher’s counterpart to this discipline, though without its intimacy with God [1]. The road continues into composure and serenity, into the detachment that loosens the grip of wanting, and into the patience and gratitude that tests and trials call forth.
subjects.arc: Open with effort and practical care, acknowledge emotional difficulty and grief, explore freedom from attachment and limits of foresight, then follow gratitude, endurance, and prayer toward loving trust.

order.why: Keep the reported insistence on treatment and vigilance beside submission.
shortened: We are submissive. If one is not submissive, then one falls into trials. "We shall surely test you with something of fear and hunger and loss of wealth and lives and fruits; but give glad tidings to the patient." Submissiveness brings great comfort to a person. One does not fall short in what is necessary and proper, whether in treatment or in vigilance. But one is submissive, otherwise how can a person find peace in this abode of accidents? One would always remain anxious. It is impossible for a day to pass without some incident. There is no peace for man except through submission.

order.why: Open with the reported union of effort and inward resignation.
shortened: He can never find peace but through effort and resignation, so that, notwithstanding all efforts in worldly affairs, the human heart remains free and happy. He neither becomes proud on attaining wealth and position nor becomes dejected on losing them.

order.why: Read striving together with trust.
shortened: Rather, trust and reliance on the divine will and purpose brings one to a place where, despite striving and endeavoring in affairs, they have no desire except for what occurs and no wish other than what comes to pass. In that state, they see all matters in accordance with their own desire and will, and consider them promoters of their honor and comfort.

order.why: Connect contentment with carrying a greater burden of service.
shortened: Sacrifice yourself, your talent, your time, your rest to another, to one who has to bear a heavier load than you - and your unhappy mood will dissolve into a blessed, contented submission to God.

order.why: Join humility to noble deeds.
shortened: Verily I pray unto my Lord with all humbleness, meekness, obedience and submissiveness--which demolisheth every edifice of self-exaltation--that He shall strengthen thee by the fragrances of holiness and the breath of the Spirit of Truth and cause thee to be dedicated (or severed) unto God, purged and purified from the dross of the world, holy and sanctified from carnal passions, sacrificing thy soul to the beloved of God, contented with that which the Lord hath granted thee in the world, anxious to perform noble and good deeds while following the teachings of God, and in all things adhering to the law of God.

order.why: Acknowledge the difficulty and intricacy of radiant acquiescence.
Retain the acknowledgment of human feelings.
shortened: In truth, were man to attain the stage of certitude in his spiritual development, no affliction could ever depress his spirits, though he would undoubtedly be influenced by reason of his human susceptibilities. Nevertheless, manis inner being will be so revived by the breeze of divinely ordained woes and trials that the dust of wailing and lamentation will entirely subside and the light of submissive resignation unto His Will shall shine forth like unto a radiant morn.

order.why: Give bereavement, tears, prayer, and patience their full setting.
shortened: O my God, my God! Thou seest me a captive of fate and destiny, immersed in the seas of tribulation and trial, prostrate upon the couch of grief and sorrow, consort to hardship, bereavement and woe. Not a day passes but I hear a herald announcing the death of one of Thy dearest loved ones, bringing news of the ascension of one of Thy chosen ones. Thus do souls fall into despair, eyes shed tears, and hearts melt in these calamities.

We have no recourse but to submit, be content, show patience and composure when destiny strikes, and resign ourselves to Thy will when trials intensify. Lord! Let not our hearts deviate after Thou hast guided us, and pour upon us patience in all circumstances and conditions. Verily, Thou art the Most Merciful, the Compassionate, the Most High.

order.why: Hear the Bab’s concern for his wife and family.
shortened: And my sorrow is for the dwellers of the house, that no grief should befall them, for otherwise there is no solace except contentment with the divine decree.

order.why: Keep the Bab’s awareness that nearness could bring affliction to others.
shortened: At all times the sorrow that hath been is but the sorrow and longing for the Presence. And though I am far removed from attaining the honour of that Presence, yet, for divers reasons -- inasmuch as my nearness would give rise to afflictions -- I am well-pleased, for my own self, with whatsoever He willeth: resignation to the decree of God and submission to His command. Only, as to drawing nigh unto the Presence, let nothing occur that would become a cause of grief.

order.why: Read counsel following the Blessed Ascension.
Keep the returning descendant of a martyr in the passage’s particular setting.
Consider the limits of knowing which desired outcomes will prove beneficial.
shortened: How often doth man flee from one thing, fixing all his hopes upon another, yet in the end it becometh apparent that the object of desire is harmful and deleterious, whereas the thing despised is the source of advantage and benefit!

Tread, therefore, the path of acquiescence and resignation. Let no hardship sadden thy heart, nor set thy hope upon any worldly gifts. Be happy and content with whatsoever God hath willed, that thy heart and soul may find tranquillity and thine inner being and conscience may experience true joy.

order.why: Read the gnat-and-storm image as a reflection on limited human plans.
shortened: All one's plans and anticipated projects can only yield results if they are in conformity with His decree. For if one's limited plans are not in keeping with this pre-ordained and divine destiny, what can a weak servant do? What can a piece of straw possibly do when faced with the tempestuous winds? How can a mere gnat resist the gusts of a tornado? So it is better and more becoming that a servant should walk this path of radiance and contentment, that he should seek whatever God hath willed for him and neither to grow dejected nor embittered nor hardened of heart.

order.why: Consider the appeal to hidden wisdom.
Place acceptance beside the source’s account of wisdom.
Keep the counsel concerning wisdom and circumstances.
shortened: Therefore the Supreme Pen has taught the station of trust and resignation. It is evident and manifest to every person of insight and understanding that whatsoever appears from God, glorified be His majesty, has proceeded and continues to proceed from the exigencies of His consummate wisdom.

order.why: Return to wisdom in accepting what unfolds.
shortened: Be content with what We have ordained and be of those who rejoice. We decree naught except with wisdom and We desire naught save what is best for Our loved ones. It behooveth every soul to be content with the decree of his Lord and to be of those who are thankful.

order.why: Counsels resignation, contentment and detachment amid difficulty.
Read the reported freedom from habitual wants.
Keep economy and honest work within the reported counsel.
shortened: The fewer the habits, the better for the man. It is a divine virtue to be satisfied with very few things. Contentment is the antidote for all the social diseases. We must live an independent life. We must never live on others like a parasitic plant. Every person must have a profession, whether it be literary or manual, and must live a clean, manly, honest life, an example of purity to be imitated by others. Contentment is the master-key to all success.

order.why: Consider the steady rill as an image of true wealth.
Read the reported example of birds and contentment.
Keep the related report of birds satisfied with crumbs.
shortened: The people of God have not at all any dependence in this world; they neither get displeased with the bitterness of the cup, nor are they happy with its sweetness.
The people of God are like the birds, who satisfy themselves with a few crumbs, and sit the whole time on the branches of the trees and sing the praises of God.

order.why: Let the humorous report about the guest and goat question extravagant desires.
Read release from fetters as inward freedom.
shortened: If thou wouldst hearken to my words, release thyself from the fetters of whatsoever cometh to pass. Nay rather, under all conditions thank thou thy loving Lord, and yield up thine affairs unto His Will that worketh as He pleaseth. This verily is better for thee than all else, in either world.

order.why: Examine attachment to one’s own will.
shortened: Seek thou my wish and forsake thine own. Thy bondage is not for my protection, but to enable me to sustain successive tribulations, and to prepare me for the trials that must needs repeatedly assail me. Perish that lover who discerneth between the pleasant and the poisonous in his love for his beloved! Be thou satisfied with what God hath destined for thee. He, verily, ruleth over thee as He willeth and pleaseth.

order.why: Distinguish divine will from personal craving.
shortened: It behooveth us to look to God's will and purpose, and to what He loveth and is pleased with, not to what our desires crave, our wills desire, and our hearts delight in. The whole matter is in His hands. It is for us to thank Him, praise Him, glorify Him, sanctify Him, mention Him, and extol Him in hardship and ease, in adversity and tribulation, and in all that cometh upon His servants in this world.

order.why: Keep freedom from dependence on opinions.
shortened: He must in no wise fix his gaze upon the tongues of men - how they move and what they utter. In all conditions he must look to the divine Command and know it to be the cause of joy and gladness, and in truth be gladdened by it. This is the station of contentment that hath been recorded and inscribed in the books of old and of latter days.

order.why: Read the counsel toward self-effacement.
Place the related exhortation beside it.
Consider the reported relation between happiness and alignment of will.
shortened: He answered: "Because all the existing things move according to my wish; therefore I do not find anything contrary to my desire; thus I have no sorrow. There is no doubt that all the beings move by the will of God, and I have given up my own will, desiring the will of God. Thus my will becomes the will of God, for there is nothing of myself. All are moving by His will, yet they are moving by my will. In this case, I am very happy."

order.why: Keep happiness within resignation.
shortened: Content with God's will, utterly resigned, my heart surrendered to whatever fate had in store, I was happy. For a boon companion, I had great joy.

order.why: Read the promise of peace in its devotional setting.
shortened: Live thou in the station of resignation and contentment so that thy heart and soul may obtain peace and serenity.

order.why: Consider the reported image of paradise in contentment.
shortened: Those souls who in this world submit to every occurrence and constantly live in a state of contentment and submission, who are satisfied and content with their destiny and never question the work of God, and who are thankful and patient - these souls dwell in the paradise of delight.

order.why: Keep the prison setting of the reported happiness.
shortened: My happiness was perfect in those dark days of imprisonment and vicissitudes. I was more happy then than now; because I had no will of my own. I was perfectly resigned.

order.why: Read the reported counsel on adapting to circumstances.
Retain the reported formulation of acceptance.
shortened: He submitted to God's decree and showed acceptance and contentment.

order.why: Read radiant acquiescence among spiritual gifts.
Consider the reciprocal language of divine and human pleasure.
shortened: Strive thou to be content, and for God to be well-pleased with thee. If thou art enabled to attain unto the word of contentment, by My life, thou shalt possess all things, for it is the crimson sulphur, and it is the greatest elixir, and it is that precious pearl whose value no assessor or appraiser can determine.

order.why: Keep the name Rida and the theme of contentment together.
Read Rida beside the tranquil soul.
shortened: O kind friend! Praise be to God that thou art designated by the name of contentment (Rida) and art content in thy heart with His decree.

The station of contentment is among the most exalted of stations, and the state of resignation is among the most excellent of states. As far as thou art able, be content and resigned, and commit all to God. Seek none but His face, follow none but His path, and speak naught but His praise, so that thou mayest become the tranquil soul, content and well-pleasing, and become accepted and beloved at the Threshold of His Oneness.

order.why: Consider the description of tranquil souls.
shortened: Be not distressed, and know with certainty that His grace has ever encompassed and will continue to encompass assured and tranquil souls who have turned to Him. All good lies in what He has willed and ordained, for He is the All-Knowing and is aware of what benefits His friends.

order.why: Keep the counsel toward calmness.
shortened: It behooveth one like thee to endure every trial, to be pleased with the decree and to commit all thy affairs to God, so that thou mayest be a calm, approved and pleasing soul before God.

order.why: Read the response to anxiety.
shortened: Therefore it behooves us to thank God at all times and be content with what He has ordained for us of His firm decrees, and not be anxious about what descends from Him, nor be disturbed by what He has decreed by His command.

order.why: Acknowledge agitation amid tests.
Keep encouragement against losing heart.
shortened: Do thou likewise neither lament nor grieve, but be content with the divine decrees and whatsoever hath been ordained by Him.
Be not disheartened - be content with the good-pleasure of the Friend.

order.why: Locate contentment among related virtues.
Join patience to forgiveness.
shortened: I hope that ye will attain the utmost patience, composure and resignation, and I entreat and implore at the Threshold of Oneness, begging for forgiveness and pardon.

order.why: Read patience with dignity.
shortened: This world contains opposites - sometimes there is abundance and sometimes hardship, sometimes joy and sometimes sorrow and tribulation, sometimes the season of youth and sometimes the time of weakness. It does not remain in one state. Therefore one must be patient, dignified, grateful and maintain an attitude of submission and contentment.

order.why: Keep fortitude alongside acceptance.
shortened: Seek contentment, show fortitude, ask for steadfastness, give your heart to God's decree. Divine wisdom has required this.

order.why: Read the direct appeal to patience.
shortened: Let not, however, thy soul grieve over that which God hath rained down upon Us. Merge thy will in His pleasure, for We have, at no time, desired anything whatsoever except His Will, and have welcomed each one of His irrevocable decrees. Let thine heart be patient, and be thou not dismayed.

order.why: Keep its further expression in adversity.
shortened: Blessed is the people that hath laid hold on the cord of patience and resignation and hath been content with God's decree, the Mighty, the Self-Subsisting.

order.why: Consider patience as sustenance.
shortened: O spiritual friend! Praise be to God that He has ordained patience and forbearance as sustenance for sincere hearts, and decreed that trials should taste as sweets to the sincere ones.

order.why: Read the image of beautiful patience.
shortened: And dear is it to Me that I should be in one land while you are in another land, and this is hard upon Me and upon every seeing lover. But We have acquiesced to God's good-pleasure and decree, and I counsel you to beautiful patience.

order.why: Return to endurance in the particular counsel.
shortened: Be thou patient and grieve not, then be content with what He hath ordained for thee, for this is better for thee than all that thou hast known or shalt know, for the matter hath been decreed and fulfilled, and We are witness to this.

order.why: Consider Maryam’s garment of resignation.
shortened: Clothe thyself with the garment of resignation, and quaff from the pure wine of contentment. Sell this world for a dirham and let thy heart be captive to the divine decree and thy soul tied to destiny.

order.why: Read the Bab’s pairing of glory and abasement, ease and hardship.
shortened: Be thou content at all times with thy Lord's decree concerning thyself, both inwardly and outwardly. The limit of contentment is that thou shouldst be as content with abasement as with glory, with poverty as with wealth, with hardship as with ease, and with sorrow as with joy in the conditions decreed for thee by God.

order.why: Place hardship and ease within one response of trust.
shortened: Now are days of hardship - be confident that the time of ease and comfort will also come. This hardship and ease, poverty and wealth, comfort and difficulty have no importance.

order.why: Read the sword of destiny in its devotional voice.
shortened: It is better that we bow our heads to the sword of destiny and offer our breasts as shields to the arrow of fate with acceptance. What recourse is there except submission and contentment?

order.why: Keep pearls and arrows as images of fidelity.
shortened: At such a time as this, through the power, the outpouring bounty and the loving providence of God one might attain such heights of acquiescence that no change, no vicissitude may affect this station. As it is written: Should He ordain pearls without price for us, let our hearts become the shells fit to treasure them. Should He rain arrows of misfortune on us, let our lives be targets to receive them.

order.why: Consider poison and honey as the language of transformed response.
shortened: To be content with His decree means that thou shouldst seek with heart and soul every tribulation in the path of God and endure with the utmost joy every affliction. Thou shouldst taste deadly poison as though it were sweet honey, and seek destructive venom as though it were pure nectar. For although these tribulations are bitter, they yield sweet fruits and bestow infinite delight.

order.why: Retain the related bitter-and-sweet formulation.
shortened: Therefore we must drink the poison of divine decree as though it were sweet honey, and eagerly seek the unerring arrow of destiny, for submission gives rise to purpose and resignation brings forth desire - until we see what God has ordained and what fate has decreed.

order.why: Read bitterness as honey within love’s imagery.
Keep the sweet cup image.
Consider trials described as bounty.
shortened: Know therefore that calamities suffered in the path of the True One are a bounty; and contentment under His decree is among the characteristics of the people of God.

order.why: Read affliction within the spiritual path.
Keep the particular great calamity in view.
shortened: We have no recourse but to submit to God's decree and to show patience and resignation in the face of this most great calamity.

order.why: Read the reported acceptance of suffering as attributed counsel.
Keep Badi’s instructions and desire for martyrdom in their historical setting.
shortened: But if [the Shah] letteth him go, and interfereth not with him, let him say, "Praise be unto Thee, O Lord of all the worlds! Verily, I am content with Thy good pleasure and what Thou hast predestined unto me in Thy path, even though I did desire that the earth might be dyed with my blood for Thy love. But what Thou willest is best for me: verily, Thou knowest what is in myself, while I know not what is in Thy Self; and Thou art the All-Knowing, the All-Informed."

order.why: Read the account of the Primal Point’s will and unknown consequences.
Keep the Herald’s contentment in its source setting.
Read the lovers’ hope in the divine decree.
shortened: Thy firm decree in Thy good-pleasure is the desire of the sincere ones, the hope of the longing ones, and the life of the lovers.

order.why: Return to hope amid the decree.
Consider the language of giving and calling back.
Keep the affirmation of divine justice.
shortened: Hold fast to the cord of submission and contentment. Verily He seeth and heareth and judgeth with justice, and He is the Just, the Wise. And he whose temple is adorned with the ornament of contentment, he is of the people of Baha in the Crimson Book.

order.why: Read the cited tradition in its theological voice.
shortened: Divine decree is beloved by the wise, and all are content with it, nay rather thankful. The complainant is not and hath never been acceptable. "Whoso is not content with My decree, let him seek another Lord."

order.why: Consider the promised better gift.
shortened: Be content with what God hath ordained for thee. He hath destined for those who desire Him that which is better for them than all else created in the contingent world.

order.why: Hear the counsel applied to the speaker’s own joy.
shortened: Be in the utmost state of submission and contentment, and follow not thy desires but rather follow what this needy servant conveyeth unto thee, for he desireth for thee naught save what he desireth for himself, and teacheth thee not a letter except by that which he hath taught himself, and remembereth thee not save by that which he remembereth his own soul, and loveth thee now as he loved thee before.
Live in the world with joy and delight, then build thy affairs upon trust in God and contentment.

order.why: Turn toward thanksgiving.
shortened: All this was decreed for Us by God, the Mighty, the Beautiful. We thank Him in all this and praise Him for all of this and for all that was ordained from His presence, and We shall be, God willing, among the patient ones.

order.why: Keep gratitude in the particular counsel.
shortened: Yet We remain thankful for this, in praiseworthy gratitude. We thank God for what He has decreed for Us of His firm and ordained destiny. By God, whatever appears from the Beloved, He indeed is the One Who is loved.

order.why: Read the enduringly grateful person.
shortened: However, if these stages occur in the path of divine good-pleasure, they are desirable and beloved, and the true lover is content in all conditions and grateful in every circumstance - this is the ultimate goal.

order.why: Consider gratitude and complaint together.
shortened: As it is said: "If you are grateful, you will be rewarded and God's decree will be carried out; and if you complain, you will be deprived and God's decree will still be carried out."

order.why: Retain thanksgiving amid tribulations.
Keep the brief expression of thanks.
shortened: The Friend hath come for the sake of meeting, and this matter hath been recorded as the greatest of deeds in the divine Books, yet due to wisdom it hath been forbidden. Therefore must all be content with His decisive command, nay rather, be thankful for whatsoever appeareth from Him.

order.why: Return to gratitude before the decree.
shortened: In any case, we are thankful - you too must be thankful.

order.why: Read praise as a response.
shortened: This is the station of contentment with God's decree and of praise and supplication to the Peerless Beloved, Who has blessed them with such a great bounty in the shelter of the Luminary of Effulgence, in the presence of the Most Great Mercy.

order.why: Keep the further praise.
Hear complaint brought into a prayer of surrender.
shortened: Therefore it would be better if, though we be complaint from head to toe and lamentation from toe to head, we should in one station die to all desires and imaginings and surrender heart and soul to His good-pleasure.

order.why: Consider the counsel against complaint.
shortened: I have not complained, nor will I complain, and I remain content with whatsoever God hath ordained for Me and whatsoever He hath prescribed for My Own Self, if ye be of those who know.

order.why: Keep restraint beside inward acceptance.
shortened: Restrain thyself from that which thou art forbidden, then be content with what hath been ordained for thee in the heaven of God, the Sovereign, the Powerful, the All-Knowing, the All-Wise.

order.why: Distinguish this disposition from idle words.
Read obedience as a practical expression.
shortened: Therefore be content with God's good-pleasure and transgress not His command. This is better for you than all that ye desire or love.

order.why: Locate acceptance within recognition.
shortened: It is incumbent upon those who have accepted to be content with the good-pleasure of the Friend and to be found submissive and obedient at the dawning of the divine Sun of the Cause.

order.why: Consider the example of the Lord.
Read the exemplar’s response.
shortened: Hence, ye must needs be in the utmost state of resignation and contentment, and in adversity and tribulation be moved to forbearance and patience, that all may follow your example and be immersed in the ocean of acquiescence.

order.why: Keep the candle of faithfulness.
Consider the image of the leaf.
shortened: This outward separation and division hath been caused by the rebellion and heedlessness of the people. Therefore that leaf must not be sorrowful, but rather content and grateful for what hath been ordained for her.

order.why: Read the ocean of loving-kindness.
shortened: God willing, drink ye in all conditions from the ocean of contentment.
The loving-kindness of God hath ever been and shall ever be with the steadfast ones who have turned unto Him.

order.why: Hear the reported assurance of belonging to God’s family.
shortened: To pray is to trust in God, and to be submissive in all things to Him. Be submissive, then things will change for you. Put your family in God's hands. Love God's will.

order.why: Keep the handmaid’s particular counsel.
shortened: It is not for me, who am a handmaid of Thine, to say, whence is this to me or wherefore hath it happened, inasmuch as Thou art glorified in all Thine acts, and art to be obeyed in Thy decree.

order.why: Read the further address to a handmaid.
Retain the concise call to acceptance.
shortened: Be content in all conditions with whatsoever hath been ordained for thee from the presence of the Mighty, the Most High.

order.why: Keep its companion counsel.
shortened: Therefore one must be content with fate and surrender to destiny, and be grateful and thankful for whatever has been ordained.

order.why: Read the brief personal exhortation.
shortened: O handmaiden of God! Be thou resigned unto fate and be satisfied with whatever the operation of destiny causeth to occur.

order.why: Retain the additional assurance.
shortened: Be content with the divine decree and set thy face toward resignation and contentment.

order.why: Keep the particular invitation to contentment.
shortened: We have no recourse except to be content with God's decree.

order.why: Read the compact formulation of surrender.
shortened: Today all must fix their gaze upon the horizon of God and, in whatsoever may come to pass, manifest complete contentment and submission.

order.why: Preserve the distinct brief counsel.
shortened: Be content with what God has decreed for us, then be patient and be of the patient ones.

order.why: Keep the next particular address.
shortened: All must be content with God's good-pleasure and be submissive to His Cause.

order.why: Read the further affirmation.
Retain the counsel on the divine will.
Keep the short expression of contentment.
shortened: Be thou content with that which thy Lord, the All-Knowing Ordainer, hath ordained.

order.why: Read the brief concluding exhortation.
shortened: O servant! Grieve not for what hath befallen thee from the decrees of fate. Be content with what God hath ordained for thee, for naught descendeth upon anyone save that which is better for him than all that hath been created between the heavens and the earth. Beware lest thou grieve in the face of destiny.

order.why: Place arrival in the ordained land within the movement toward prayer.
shortened: We have arrived in the land which God hath ordained for Us, and We are content with whatsoever God hath been pleased to decree for Us, and submissive to that which He hath destined from His presence, and thankful for that which He hath ordained from His court.

order.why: Read trust and thanksgiving for the Tablet.
shortened: Adorn thyself with the ornament of trust, resignation and submission, and say: My God, my God! Praise be unto Thee for having remembered me in Thy Most Great Prison, and thanksgiving be unto Thee for having revealed unto me that which shall endure as long as Thy dominion and Thy kingdom, Thy glory and Thy sovereignty shall endure, O God of the worlds!

order.why: Keep joy at receiving the Tablet.
shortened: God willing, thou shalt attain unto this blessed Tablet and be blessed with such joy that the tribulations of the world shall not make thee sorrowful, and in all conditions thou shalt remain content and thankful, uttering "Praise be unto Thee, O Lord of the worlds."

order.why: Enter the prayer for this disposition.
Read the prayer of acceptance.
shortened: Then cause me, O my God, to be content with whatsoever Thou hast ordained for me through Thy grace and bounty and generosity and favors.

order.why: Hear the servant’s supplication.
shortened: Be content with God's decree. Say: O my Lord! I am Thy servant and the son of Thy servant. I am content with what hath befallen me in Thy days.

order.why: Join resignation to the request to become worthy helpers.
Keep the prayer for steadiness.
Read the healing prayer beside practical care at the opening.
shortened: So do with me as You wish, and ordain for me as You wish, and make easy for me as You wish, and expand my breast as You wish. Heal me if Your will desires it, and cure me if Your purpose agrees to it, for I desire nothing except what You desire.

order.why: Retain the personal prayerful appeal.
shortened: Beseech God that in all conditions thou mayest be successful in attaining His good-pleasure and be content with His decree.

order.why: Read the prayer before the decree.
Keep the Dove’s devotional imagery.
shortened: I beseech Thee by the cooing of the Dove of Thy Cause to make me content in all conditions with what Thou hast ordained for me through Thy decree and destiny.

order.why: Let the short prayer gather the theme.
shortened: O Lord! Make me content with what Thou hast ordained for me. Thou art, verily, the Mighty, the All-Forgiving.

order.why: Read the further supplication.
Keep the prayer in tribulation.
shortened: Say: Baha doth not await deliverance from the tribulations ordained for Him, nor doth He seek release, but saith: "O my God! Shouldst Thou desire, remove me from these horizons, that the people of hypocrisy--who have denied the Day of Separation and broken the Covenant--may no longer behold me. O Lord! Thou knowest what is within my soul and beholdest my dwelling place. Decree, then, what Thou willest. By Thy glory! What Thou hast purposed is my purpose, and what Thou hast desired is my desire in this world and the next."

order.why: Close with the relation of friend and Friend.
shortened: What befitteth the friend is submission to, and contentment with, the good-pleasure of the Friend. The Friend saith: "My friend, thou wilt surely love that which I love." Therefore, be thou content with the good-pleasure of the Friend and with whatsoever proceedeth from Him.

questions: How do the passages joining effort, vigilance, and resignation change the meaning of contentment?
What room do these readings leave for grief, anxiety, and the gradual growth of a tranquil heart?
How might gratitude alter our relationship to desire without diminishing care for practical needs?
What do images of sweetness in bitterness illuminate, and where does their personal or historical setting matter?
How does Epictetus’s distinction between what we control and what we do not compare with these prayers of trust in God?
What might contentment contribute to service, and what would help us recognize when acceptance has become an excuse for inaction?
